lobsterBriefs.headline: Taiwan watches the treaty from outside the room
lobsterBriefs.body: Taiwan isn't a UN member, so it doesn't get a seat at the plastic treaty table. But Taiwan's environment ministry says it will follow the treaty's rules anyway, once those rules are decided.
lobsterBriefs.whyItMatters: Treaties don't only matter for the countries inside the room. They set the new normal for everyone.

lobsterBriefs.headline: Taiwan's plan to phase out four plastics
lobsterBriefs.body: Taiwan has a roadmap to slowly get rid of four single-use plastic things — bags, straws, forks/spoons, and drink cups — first in schools and offices, then in shops, then everywhere. The end goal: a full ban.

lobsterBriefs.headline: More shops, fewer free plastic bags
lobsterBriefs.body: In 2018 Taiwan added seven more kinds of shops — like bakeries and pharmacies — to the list of stores that can't hand out free plastic bags. If you want one, you pay.

lobsterBriefs.headline: Uni-President: lighter bottles, more recycled PET
lobsterBriefs.body: Uni-President is one of Taiwan's biggest food and drink companies. They say they're using more recycled PET (that's old plastic melted down for new bottles) and making each bottle a tiny bit lighter.

lobsterBriefs.headline: Formosa Plastics: the giant that makes the plastic
lobsterBriefs.body: Formosa Plastics is one of the biggest companies in the world that actually makes brand-new plastic from oil. They publish reports about going greener — but environmental groups say those promises don't yet include making less plastic in the first place.
lobsterBriefs.whyItMatters: If a company makes plastic for a living, asking them to make less plastic is asking them to change their whole business. That's why the treaty fight is so hard.
